title: Locke, Berkeley and Hume
objective: After this level you can explain the empiricist claim that all ideas come from experience, from Locke's blank slate to Berkeley and Hume.
summary: Locke called the newborn mind a blank slate filled by experience, Berkeley said to be is to be perceived, and Hume made every idea a copy of an impression; Leibniz answered with veined marble.

cards.headline: Where did your idea of a golden mountain come from?
cards.body: You’ve never seen one, yet you can picture it instantly. David Hume said that picture is still built entirely from experience.

cards.headline: The blank slate
cards.body: John Locke’s Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689) argued that we have no innate knowledge. At birth the mind is a blank slate, and all ideas, the materials of knowledge, come from experience: sensation of the world outside, and reflection on the workings of our own minds.

cards.headline: To be is to be perceived
cards.body: George Berkeley went further. An apple, he said, is a collection of ideas: a colour, taste, smell, shape and firmness that go together. There’s no mind-independent matter behind them. To be is to be perceived. Critics asked whether a tree in an empty college quad stops existing; one answer Berkeley suggests is that God always perceives it.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: Berkeley didn’t deny that apples exist. He denied they exist apart from minds.

cards.headline: Copies of impressions
cards.body: Hume split our perceptions in two: lively impressions, when we see, hear, feel or desire, and fainter ideas, which copy them. A golden mountain just joins two ideas you already had, gold and mountain. Hume even offered an exception: someone who had seen every shade of blue but one could probably imagine the missing shade.

cards.headline: Veins in the marble
cards.body: Rationalists weren’t convinced the mind starts empty. Against Locke’s blank slate, Leibniz offered a different image: a block of marble whose veins help decide which figures can be carved from it. The mind, on this view, helps determine what it can take in.

cards.headline: Locke, Berkeley and Hume: the big picture
learned: Locke: the mind starts as a blank slate
Berkeley: to be is to be perceived
Hume: every idea copies an impression
Leibniz: the mind is veined marble

questions.prompt: The image John Locke used for the mind at birth was _____.

options.label: a mirror
options.rationale: Locke’s image was of something empty, waiting to be filled.

questions.explanation: Locke said the newborn mind is a blank slate: all its ideas come from experience.

questions.prompt: Which Indian school from Level 9 comes closest to the empiricists’ trust in experience?

options.label: Advaita Vedanta, which says the self is Brahman
options.rationale: That’s a claim about the self, not about sources of knowledge.

options.label: The Jains, with their many-sided truth
The Carvakas, who accepted perception alone as reliable
The Buddhists, with their chariot
options.rationale: That argument is about the self.

questions.explanation: The Carvakas trusted perception alone, echoing the empiricist view that knowledge comes from experience.
